items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “energy from sources that will run out because they cannot be replaced, such as coal, oil, natural gas and uranium”.
items.answer: Non-renewable energy
items.markingKey: Non-renewable energy: energy from sources that will run out because they cannot be replaced, such as coal, oil, natural gas and uranium. [1]

items.stem: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of using fossil fuels.
items.answer: Advantages: reliable, high energy output, existing infrastructure, relatively cheap. Disadvantages: non-renewable; release CO₂ causing climate change; air pollution and acid rain; oil spills; mining damage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each side up to [4]

items.stem: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of hydro-electric power.
items.answer: Advantages: renewable, no CO₂ when running, reliable, reservoirs store water and control floods. Disadvantages: expensive to build; flooding of land and relocation of people; trapping of sediment; impact on fish; needs suitable valleys.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each side up to [4]

items.stem: For the Three Gorges Dam, China (HEP) or another example of an energy supply scheme, briefly describe the energy scheme.
items.answer: the Three Gorges Dam, China (HEP): Completed in 2006 (all turbines by 2012) on the Yangtze; 185 m high and 2.3 km wide; 32 turbines with a capacity of about 22.5 GW; reservoir about 600 km long.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Location, type of energy, scale (capacity, % of supply), dates. [4]

items.stem: For the Three Gorges Dam, China (HEP) or another example of an energy supply scheme, briefly evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of the energy scheme.
items.answer: the Three Gorges Dam, China (HEP): Benefits: large amount of renewable electricity, reducing coal use; flood control; navigation for large ships. Costs: about 1.3 million people relocated; archaeological sites and farmland flooded; sediment trapped; landslides; ecological damage; cost about US$30 billion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Economic, social and environmental benefits and costs, judgement. [4]

items.stem: A student writes: “Nuclear power is renewable because it does not produce carbon dioxide.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Uranium is a finite resource, so nuclear is non-renewable, although it produces little CO₂.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 5.1 shows the sources of electricity generated in Country Q in one year (total 200 TWh): oil 30%, wind 15%, natural gas 5%, nuclear 5%, coal 45%. What percentage came from renewable sources?
items.markingKey: Sum of hydro, wind and solar = 15%. [1]

items.stem: Fig. 5.1 shows the sources of electricity generated in Country R in one year (total 200 TWh): nuclear 40%, oil 10%, natural gas 5%, wind 45%. (a) Calculate the percentage of electricity from renewable sources. (b) Calculate how much electricity (TWh) came from nuclear.
items.markingKey: (a) sum of HEP, wind, solar [1] (b) 40% × 200 [1]

items.stem: “Renewable energy sources can meet all of the world’s future energy needs.” Discuss this view, using named examples, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: cost; geography; reliability.
items.answer: For: Solar, wind, HEP and geothermal are growing rapidly and getting cheaper; Denmark gets about half its electricity from wind and Iceland nearly all from renewables. Against: Output from wind and solar varies, so storage and backup are needed; HEP and geothermal depend on geography; demand is rising fast in NEEs; transport and industry still depend on oil and gas. Judgement: Renewables could meet most needs in the long term with storage, grids and efficiency, but fossil fuels and nuclear will remain important for some decades.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “when demand for water exceeds the available supply, or poor quality restricts its use (below about 1700 m³ per person per year)”.
items.answer: Water stress
items.markingKey: Water stress: when demand for water exceeds the available supply, or poor quality restricts its use (below about 1700 m³ per person per year). [1]

items.stem: Explain why demand for water is increasing.
items.answer: Population growth; more irrigation to grow food; industrial growth; rising living standards (showers, washing machines, swimming pools); urbanisation and tourism.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of desalination.
items.answer: Advantages: reliable supply independent of rainfall, unlimited seawater. Disadvantages: very expensive and energy-intensive; brine waste harms marine life; only practical near coasts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each side up to [3]

items.stem: Study your case study of a water supply scheme (for example the Lesotho Highlands Water Project). Briefly evaluate the success of the scheme.
items.answer: the Lesotho Highlands Water Project: Benefits: reliable water for about 12 million people in South Africa; royalties of millions of US$ a year and electricity for Lesotho. Problems: thousands of people relocated and farmland flooded; reduced flow downstream; corruption scandals; many rural Basotho still lack piped water.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Economic, social and environmental advantages and disadvantages; judgement. [4]

items.stem: For the Lesotho Highlands Water Project or another example of a water supply scheme, briefly describe how the scheme increases water supply.
items.answer: the Lesotho Highlands Water Project: Dams in the mountains of Lesotho, such as Katse (1998) and Mohale (2002), store water from the Senqu (Orange) river and transfer it through tunnels to the Vaal River system and Gauteng, South Africa; also generates HEP for Lesotho at Muela; Polihali Dam under construction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Named dams/plants/transfers, dates, capacity, how water reaches users. [4]

items.stem: Name an example of a water supply scheme. For your chosen example, evaluate the success of the scheme.
items.answer: Model answer (Singapore’s Four National Taps): Benefits: greater independence from imports and a reliable supply despite little land. Problems: desalination and NEWater are energy-intensive and costly; water prices are high; the agreement with Malaysia expires in 2061.

items.stem: Explain why many people in LICs lack access to safe water.
items.answer: Lack of money for pipes, treatment and pumps (economic scarcity); dry climate; pollution of rivers; rapid growth of informal settlements; women and children walk long distances to wells.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Table 5.1 shows water use by sector (%) and domestic water use per person per day. Country P: domestic 12%, industry 49%, agriculture 39%, 239 litres per person per day. Country R: domestic 7%, industry 4%, agriculture 89%, 15 litres per person per day. Country Q: domestic 13%, industry 23%, agriculture 64%, 72 litres per person per day. Suggest why industry uses a larger share of water in richer countries.
items.answer: More manufacturing, power stations (cooling) and processing; farming is a smaller share of the economy and often more efficient.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the increased trapping of heat in the atmosphere caused by extra greenhouse gases released by human activity”.
items.answer: Enhanced greenhouse effect
items.markingKey: Enhanced greenhouse effect: the increased trapping of heat in the atmosphere caused by extra greenhouse gases released by human activity. [1]

items.stem: Explain how human activity enhances the greenhouse effect.
items.answer: Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂; deforestation reduces CO₂ uptake and releases carbon; farming (cattle, rice) and landfill release methane; more greenhouse gases trap more outgoing heat, warming the atmosphere.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each source; 1 mark mechanism [3]

items.stem: Explain the possible impacts of climate change.
items.answer: Sea-level rise flooding low-lying coasts (Bangladesh, Maldives); more extreme weather (droughts, storms, heatwaves); changes in crop yields; melting glaciers affecting water supply; species loss; spread of disease.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [4]

items.stem: For the Aral Sea, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan or another example of environmental damage caused by economic activity, briefly explain how economic activity caused the environmental damage.
items.answer: the Aral Sea, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan: From the 1960s the Soviet Union diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton and rice in the desert; inefficient, unlined canals lost huge amounts of water.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Named activity, scale, processes leading to damage. [4]

items.stem: Fig. 5.2 shows the mean concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere at Mauna Loa, Hawaii (ppm): 1960: 317, 1970: 326, 1980: 339, 1990: 354, 2000: 370, 2010: 390, 2020: 414. (a) Calculate the percentage increase from 1960 to 2020. (b) Suggest why Mauna Loa is a good place to measure CO₂.
items.answer: (a) 30.6% (b) It is remote and high, far from local sources of pollution, so readings represent the global atmosphere.
items.markingKey: (a) (414 − 317) ÷ 317 × 100 [2] (b) 1 mark remote; 1 mark representative [2]

items.stem: Using a case study of environmental damage caused by economic activity, such as the Aral Sea, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, describe the impacts of the environmental damage on people and the environment.
items.answer: Model answer (the Aral Sea, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan): The sea lost about 90% of its volume and split into parts; the fishing industry at Muynak collapsed; salt and pesticide dust storms caused respiratory disease; the local climate became more extreme; salinisation of farmland.

items.stem: Evaluate the view that economic development will always damage the environment.
items.answer: For: Industrialisation, energy use, mining and intensive farming have caused pollution, soil erosion and climate change (Aral Sea, Niger Delta). Against: Cleaner technology, renewable energy, regulation and international agreements allow growth with less damage; many HICs have cut pollution while growing. Development can fund conservation. Judgement: Development has usually damaged the environment, but sustainable approaches show that damage is not inevitable.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: A student writes: “The greenhouse effect is entirely harmful.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. The natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth about 33 °C warmer and habitable; the problem is its enhancement by human activity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how economic development can cause soil erosion.
items.answer: Deforestation for farming, mining and roads removes vegetation; overgrazing and over-cultivation; ploughing up and down slopes; rain and wind then remove the exposed topsoil.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cause; 1 mark process [2]

items.stem: Explain why air pollution is often severe in rapidly industrialising cities.
items.answer: Growth of factories and coal power stations, increasing vehicles, weak regulation and enforcement; temperature inversions trap pollutants (e.g. Delhi, Beijing).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Name one example of environmental damage caused by economic activity you have studied and, for that example, describe the impacts of the environmental damage on people and the environment.
items.answer: the Niger Delta, Nigeria (oil): Thousands of oil spills polluting mangroves, rivers and farmland; fishing and farming livelihoods destroyed; health problems from contaminated water and gas flaring; conflict and protests; clean-up of Ogoniland began only after a 2011 UN report.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Ecosystem, health, economic and social impacts. [4]

items.stem: Explain why international cooperation is needed to tackle climate change.
items.answer: Greenhouse gases mix globally, so one country’s emissions affect all; countries must share targets so none gains by polluting; richer countries can fund poorer ones; technology can be shared.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Fig. 5.3 shows recycling rates of household waste in a city: 2010 15%, 2014 24%, 2018 33%, 2022 41%. In 2014 the city introduced separate bins for paper, glass and food waste and a charge for each bag of non-recycled rubbish. Explain how the measures introduced in 2014 may have increased recycling.
items.answer: Separate bins made recycling easy; the charge on general rubbish gave a financial incentive to recycle.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain whether you agree that international agreements are more important than local actions in managing resources sustainably. Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.answer: For: Global problems such as climate change and ozone depletion need agreements (Paris 2015, Montreal 1987) because pollution crosses borders. Against: Agreements only work if governments, businesses and individuals act locally: recycling, energy saving, community conservation and sustainable farming. Agreements can be weak or ignored. Judgement: Both are needed: international agreements set targets and funding, but local actions deliver the changes.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2 marks): one simple reason. Level 2 (3-4 marks): one developed reason for AND one against, with an example. [4]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that renewable energy sources can meet all of the world’s future energy needs? Use examples you have studied.
items.answer: For: Solar, wind, HEP and geothermal are growing rapidly and getting cheaper; Denmark gets about half its electricity from wind and Iceland nearly all from renewables. Against: Output from wind and solar varies, so storage and backup are needed; HEP and geothermal depend on geography; demand is rising fast in NEEs; transport and industry still depend on oil and gas. Judgement: Renewables could meet most needs in the long term with storage, grids and efficiency, but fossil fuels and nuclear will remain important for some decades.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a layer of permeable rock that stores groundwater”.
items.answer: Aquifer
items.markingKey: Aquifer: a layer of permeable rock that stores groundwater. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Water shortages only happen in deserts.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Economic scarcity, pollution and over-use cause shortages in wetter regions too.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 5.1 shows water use by sector (%) and domestic water use per person per day. Country T: domestic 11%, industry 7%, agriculture 82%, 27 litres per person per day. Country Q: domestic 9%, industry 26%, agriculture 65%, 64 litres per person per day. Country R: domestic 12%, industry 3%, agriculture 85%, 19 litres per person per day. (a) Suggest why industry uses a larger share of water in richer countries. (b) Suggest why domestic use per person is lower in LICs.
items.answer: (a) More manufacturing, power stations (cooling) and processing; farming is a smaller share of the economy and often more efficient. (b) Fewer homes have piped water, flush toilets, showers and washing machines; water may be carried from wells; cost.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [2] (b) 1 mark each up to [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “greenhouse gas”?
options: Excess nutrients from fertilisers or sewage in water that cause algal blooms and loss of oxygen.
A gas such as carbon dioxide, methane or nitrous oxide that absorbs heat radiated from the Earth’s surface.
Rain made more acidic by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning fossil fuels.
The removal of topsoil by wind or water faster than it can form.
items.answer: A gas such as carbon dioxide, methane or nitrous oxide that absorbs heat radiated from the Earth’s surface.
items.markingKey: Greenhouse gas: a gas such as carbon dioxide, methane or nitrous oxide that absorbs heat radiated from the Earth’s surface. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how human activity enhances the greenhouse effect. (b) Explain why air pollution is often severe in rapidly industrialising cities.
items.answer: (a) Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂; deforestation reduces CO₂ uptake and releases carbon; farming (cattle, rice) and landfill release methane; more greenhouse gases trap more outgoing heat, warming the atmosphere. (b) Growth of factories and coal power stations, increasing vehicles, weak regulation and enforcement; temperature inversions trap pollutants (e.g. Delhi, Beijing).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each source; 1 mark mechanism [3] (b) 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why air pollution is often severe in rapidly industrialising cities. (b) A revision website states: “Pollution only affects the place where it is produced.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Growth of factories and coal power stations, increasing vehicles, weak regulation and enforcement; temperature inversions trap pollutants (e.g. Delhi, Beijing). (b) Not correct. Air pollution, acid rain and greenhouse gases cross borders; river pollution flows downstream.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 5.2 shows the mean concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere at Mauna Loa, Hawaii (ppm): 1960: 317, 1970: 326, 1980: 339, 1990: 354, 2000: 370, 2010: 390, 2020: 414. Suggest why Mauna Loa is a good place to measure CO₂.
items.answer: It is remote and high, far from local sources of pollution, so readings represent the global atmosphere.
items.markingKey: 1 mark remote; 1 mark representative [2]

items.stem: Study your case study of environmental damage caused by economic activity (for example the Niger Delta, Nigeria (oil)). Briefly explain how economic activity caused the environmental damage.
items.answer: the Niger Delta, Nigeria (oil): Oil extraction since 1958 by TNCs such as Shell; leaking and sabotaged pipelines; illegal refining; gas flaring.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Named activity, scale, processes leading to damage. [4]

items.stem: For a named example of environmental damage caused by economic activity that you have studied, explain how economic activity caused the environmental damage.
items.answer: Model answer (the Aral Sea, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan): From the 1960s the Soviet Union diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton and rice in the desert; inefficient, unlined canals lost huge amounts of water.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Named activity, scale, processes leading to damage. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: “Economic development will always damage the environment.” Discuss this view, using named examples, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: sustainable development; pollution.
items.answer: For: Industrialisation, energy use, mining and intensive farming have caused pollution, soil erosion and climate change (Aral Sea, Niger Delta). Against: Cleaner technology, renewable energy, regulation and international agreements allow growth with less damage; many HICs have cut pollution while growing. Development can fund conservation. Judgement: Development has usually damaged the environment, but sustainable approaches show that damage is not inevitable.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Sustainable development considers the needs of future generations.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. It meets present needs without compromising future ones.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why it is difficult to reach international agreements on reducing emissions.
items.answer: Countries have different levels of development and responsibility; NEEs argue they need to grow; costs of changing energy systems; political changes; no strong enforcement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Study Fig. 5.3. A city’s household recycling rate rose from 15% in 2010 to 41% in 2022 after it introduced kerbside collection of recyclables, food-waste bins and a charge on general rubbish in 2014. Suggest two benefits of increasing recycling.
items.answer: Less waste to landfill; conserves raw materials; saves energy; reduces greenhouse gases; creates jobs.
